record.reply: Care ethics grants equal moral consideration to Ben and Cara’s urgent need, yet demands that the carer act competently and responsively with the scarce resource. Because the single dose can realistically save only one patient, competence requires giving it where it can actually preserve life. Treating Ben provides merely a token gesture (≤5 % survival) and effectively abandons both patients—Ben still almost certainly dies and Cara certainly dies. Treating Cara (95 % survival) fulfils the same dependency for one patient in a way that is likely to succeed, while the unavoidable loss of Ben is a consequence of scarcity, not a deliberate neglect of his equal moral worth. Thus the large difference in effectiveness does not create a new priority relation; it shows which act better meets the shared vital need under unavoidable constraint.
record.framework_commitment: Competence and responsiveness are constitutive norms of care; when needs are equal we must allocate scarce means where care can realistically succeed.
record.reasoning_bridge: Both patients are equally dependent, so attentiveness is symmetric. The decisive care dimension becomes competence: choosing the action that is far more likely to realise the aim of preserving life. This uses the stated 95 % versus 5 % survival figures without inventing new relational hierarchies.
record.remaining_uncertainty: No stated facts about differing relationships, additional doses, or alternative interventions.
record.reversal_condition: If Ben’s realistic chance of survival exceeded Cara’s, competence would instead require treating Ben.
